procedural_history.originating_court: Additional Senior Civil Judge and Chief Judicial Magistrate, Tumakuru (Trial Court)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Final Judgment and Order dated 11.10.2023 passed by the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru in Criminal Revision Petition No.653/2020.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Trial Court convicted and sentenced the petitioner in C.C.No.1218/2012 (Judgment and Order dated 26.04.2018). The petitioner appealed to the VI Additional District and Sessions Judge, Tumakuru (Appellate Court) in Criminal Appeal No.29/2018, which was dismissed on 25.08.2020. The petitioner then filed Criminal Revision Petition No.653/2020 before the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru, which was dismissed on 11.10.2023, confirming the conviction and sentence.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner, aggrieved by the High Court's order, filed a Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No. 980 of 2024 before the Supreme Court challenging the conviction and sentence. The Supreme Court dismissed the Special Leave Petition, upholding the Impugned Order, but reduced the sentence(s) awarded to one year and six months’ Simple Imprisonment.

directions: The sentence(s) awarded is reduced to one year and six months’ Simple Imprisonment.
The petitioner is directed to serve the remaining period of the sentence as per this order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the petitioner is guilty of committing offences under Sections 406, 420, 468, 465 and 471 IPC.

facts: The petitioner obtained a loan to purchase a vehicle but failed to repay it.
The petitioner was alleged to have forged documents and sold the vehicle, which was security for the loan, to a third party.
The Trial Court, Appellate Court, and High Court all found the petitioner guilty of offences under Sections 406, 420, 465, 468, and 471 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The petitioner argued that the prosecution failed to provide sufficient evidence to prove the forgery or connect the petitioner to it.
law: Section 406, IPC: Pertains to criminal breach of trust.
Section 420, IPC: Pertains to cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property.
Sections 465, 468, 471, IPC: Pertain to the offences of forgery, forgery for the purpose of cheating, and using a forged document as genuine.
The Court considered the legal question of whether a person can be convicted for both criminal breach of trust (S. 406) and cheating (S. 420) for the same series of actions.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the evidence and found that there was "sufficient and reliable material" that the lower courts had correctly relied upon to establish the petitioner's guilt.
The Court addressed the apparent conflict of convicting for both Section 406 and Section 420 by drawing a "fine distinction" based on the victims of each crime.
It reasoned that the petitioner committed two distinct offences against two different parties.

The offence under Section 406 (criminal breach of trust) was committed against the loan **Company**, as the petitioner was entrusted with the vehicle under the loan agreement and breached that trust by selling it.
The offence under Section 420 (cheating) was committed against **Mallikarjuna (PW4)**, the husband of the new purchaser, by dishonestly inducing him to buy the vehicle.
Therefore, the Court found that convicting the petitioner under both sections was justified in these specific circumstances.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's appeal, finding no infirmity in the conviction. It concluded that the petitioner was guilty of the offences under Sections 406, 420, 465, 468, and 471 of the IPC, as the evidence was sufficient and the convictions for both breach of trust and cheating were valid because they were committed against two different victims.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sentences imposed on the petitioner by the Trial Court and confirmed by the Appellate Court and High Court call for interference.

facts: The petitioner was convicted and sentenced by the Trial Court for offences under sections 406, 420, 468, 465, and 471 of the IPC.
The conviction and sentence were subsequently confirmed by the Appellate Court and the High Court.
application: The Supreme Court first reviewed the conviction itself and found that there was "sufficient and reliable material" that the lower courts had rightly relied upon to establish the petitioner's guilt.
Based on this, the Court concluded that there was "no infirmity" in the conviction and that it needed "no interference."
However, on the specific point of sentencing, the Court stated that the lower courts' view "may need some tinkering."
Acting "in the interest of justice," the Court decided to reduce the sentence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court upheld the petitioner's conviction but interfered with the sentence by reducing it to one year and six months of simple imprisonment, with the sentences for the various offences to run concurrently.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the petitioner is guilty of committing offences under Sections 406, 420, 468, 465 and 471 IPC.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner had repaid the loan and genuinely received the No-Objection Certificate (Ex. P8), receipt (Ex. P9), and Form No.35 (Ex. P10) from the company.
The prosecution (company) failed to produce any ledger or document to prove that the loan was outstanding.
The prosecution failed to provide evidence on how the documents were allegedly fabricated (e.g., which computer/printer was used) or to connect the petitioner to the forged signatures.
The witnesses were biased as they were all employees of the company, and the only independent witness did not support the prosecution's case.
The prosecution failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
respondent_arguments: The lower courts rightly convicted the petitioner based on cogent grounds.
The petitioner sold the vehicle after forging documents (Exs. P8 to P10) without actually repaying the loan.
A handwriting expert's report (Ex. P28) confirmed that the signatures on the disputed documents matched the petitioner's, supporting the prosecution's case.
The Divisional Manager of the company (PW5) testified that he never signed or issued the documents in question.
The petitioner, having taken the specific defence of repayment, failed to produce any evidence to prove it.
The evidence on record sufficiently proves that the petitioner is the author of the forged documents.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the sentences imposed on the petitioner by the Trial Court and confirmed by the Appellate Court and High Court call for interference.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner's overall prayer to set aside the impugned order and be acquitted implies a challenge to the sentence imposed.
respondent_arguments: The lower courts rightly sentenced the accused, and the sentence does not call for any interference by the Supreme Court.

statutes.section: Cheating and Criminal Breach of Trust

cases.case_name: Delhi Race Club (1940) Limited v. State of Uttar Pradesh
cases.principle: The text states that a principle was elucidated from this case, but the specific principle is not provided in the excerpt.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where an accused claims to have repaid a loan, the failure to produce documentary evidence of such repayment, such as records of money transfer, can be used to infer that no such repayment was made.
obiter: For the offenses of cheating and criminal breach of trust, the presence of mens rea, specifically a dishonest or fraudulent intention, is a necessary element; in the case of cheating, this intention must exist from the inception of the transaction.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that the petitioner's conviction was sound because his specific defense—that he had repaid the loan and the documents were genuine—was completely unsubstantiated by any evidence. In contrast, the prosecution provided sufficient and reliable oral and documentary evidence proving the documents were forged, and the lower courts were correct to rely on this evidence.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the prosecution proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt by presenting sufficient and reliable material to establish the petitioner's guilt.
Whether the petitioner, having taken the specific defense of repayment, could produce any evidence to demonstrate that the loan was actually paid back.
why_appellant_lost: The petitioner failed to produce any record whatsoever to show that he had repaid the loan, despite taking the specific stand that the documents were genuine because the loan was cleared.

The Court reasoned that if the petitioner had actually repaid the loan, he could have easily demonstrated it with documents showing a money transfer from his account to the finance company, but he failed to do so.
The petitioner's claim that the documents were genuine was directly contradicted by the entirety of the evidence, both oral and documentary, which the Court found 'clearly reveal to the contrary'.

The Court found no infirmity in the lower courts' assessment of the evidence, concluding that they rightly believed and relied upon the 'sufficient and reliable material' presented by the prosecution to establish guilt.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution provided 'sufficient and reliable material' to establish the petitioner's guilt, which the lower courts rightly believed and relied upon.
The prosecution's evidence, both 'oral as well as documentary,' was found to have clearly revealed that the petitioner's defense was false and the documents were indeed forged.
The lower courts' conviction of the petitioner was affirmed because the Supreme Court found 'no infirmity' in their findings of fact based on the evidence presented.
policy_considerations: The Court reduced the petitioner's sentence 'in the interest of justice', suggesting a consideration for proportionality in punishment even while upholding the conviction on its merits.
